label: Map Outward
notes: Open by repositioning Chapter 9. The previous eight chapters built algorithms, predicates, and data structures. This closing chapter is the course's map outward: a curated landscape of bibliographies, FAQs, textbooks, collections, monographs, journals, conferences, and software, organized so a student can keep learning after the book ends. The deck follows printed pages 347 through 367.

label: Why a Source Chapter Belongs Here
notes: Explain the rationale before listing categories. Computational geometry was young enough in the source era that primary literature mattered heavily. Algorithms in the rest of the book are stated cleanly, but their robustness, degeneracy handling, and practical variants live in papers and code. Frame this lecture as a reading-and-tooling discipline rather than a theorem dump.

label: Eight Resource Categories
notes: Walk through the eight resource categories the chapter names. Each has a different job: bibliographies are for discovery, FAQs for folklore, textbooks for sustained narrative, collections for surveys, monographs for depth, journals and conferences for the frontier, and software for executable artifacts. Resist treating the list as a flat directory; insist on the role each one plays.

label: Three Practical Entry Points
notes: Highlight the three practical entry points the chapter emphasizes: handbook surveys, community bibliographies, and software directories. These are the places a working practitioner actually starts when they need to find variants, related work, or an implementation. Position them as orthogonal: one for big-picture orientation, one for paper-level discovery, and one for executable tooling.

label: Topic-Source Routing Matrix
notes: Use the matrix as a decision aid: given one of the course topics, which source category answers it first? Triangulation and hulls have textbook-level coverage. Voronoi and arrangements benefit from monographs and surveys. Motion planning needs conferences and software. The point is not to memorize the matrix but to teach the habit of asking the routing question.

label: Software Ledger and Robustness Caution
notes: Slow down on software. A robust hull or Voronoi package, a geometry class library, and reference code from textbooks each solve different things. Library abstractions must match the predicates used in the proof. Even an exact-arithmetic backend does not absolve the user from understanding degeneracy conventions, orientation tests, and numeric ranges.

label: Historical Timeline
notes: Show the source-span timeline. Annual symposia begin in the mid-1980s. Specialized textbooks and arrangements treatments appear shortly after. Handbook collections arrive in the late 1990s. Software libraries mature in parallel. The timeline argues for why the chapter foregrounds proceedings: many central results lived in conferences before consolidating into books.

label: Three-Source Reading Path Lab
notes: Walk through the applied lab. Pick one algorithm family, then build a three-step reading path: a textbook account for definitions and core proofs, a handbook or survey for variants and applications, and a software documentation page for degeneracy and precision conventions. Use Voronoi diagrams or arrangements as the worked example; both have all three layers.

label: Recap: Sources as a Toolkit
notes: Close the deck by restating the chapter's main move. Sources are a toolkit, not a directory. Bibliographies and FAQs help with discovery. Textbooks and collections give coherent explanations. Monographs add depth. Journals and conferences carry the frontier. Software turns theory into reusable machinery, but only when predicates, degeneracies, and data-structure assumptions stay visible to the user.
